newsitem.title: USA: Fromer S&L chief Keating released from prison.
newsitem.headline: Fromer S&L chief Keating released from prison.

text.p: Former Lincoln Savings and Loan chief Charles Keating was released from prison on Thursday after a federal judge ordered him freed on $300,000 bail.

Keating, wearing a dark suit and tie, emerged from the federal correctional facility in Tucson, Arizona, shortly before 5 p.m. PDT (8 p.m. EDT). He was believed to be headed to his son-in-law's house in Phoenix.

Earlier, U.S. District Court Judge Mariana Pfaelzer in Los Angeles ordered him freed on bail pending a decision on his request for a new trial on federal fraud and racketeering charges. Under terms of his release, Keating must restrict his travel to California, Arizona and Illinois, where his lawyer is based.
Pfaelzer made the ruling after a day-long meeting with jurors from Keating's federal trial three years ago.
Keating's attorneys have argued that some knew about Keating's earlier state conviction and discussed it during their deliberations.
Keating, who was serving a 12-year sentence, became a symbol of the U.S. savings and loan crisis in the 1980s when American Continental's Lincoln Savings and Loan declared bankruptcy in 1989.

The collapse had a domino effect on America's thrift industry, as hundreds of other savings and loan institutions followed Lincoln into bankruptcy. Lincoln's failure cost U.S. taxpayers $2.6 billion, making it one of the most costly failures in U.S. history.

His release was the latest in a string of legal setbacks to prosecutors who had portrayed Keating and his son Charles Keating III as greedy men who arranged phony land deals and bilked elderly investors out of millions of dollars.
His son is also currently free on bail.

In 1993, Keating was convicted on 73 federal counts of securities and wire fraud, conspiracy and racketeering, and ordered to pay $122 million in restitution. Two years earlier he was convicted in state court on 17 counts of defrauding investors.

In April, however, U.S. District Court Judge John Davies overturned the state convictions and ordered a new trial after determining the original trial judge gave improper instructions to the jury. The state is appealing Davies' ruling.

Last June, prosecutors suffered another defeat when Keating, 73, was granted a new hearing on the federal charges. An Appeals Court said Pfaelzer was wrong when she denied a defence motion to hold a hearing on allegations that jurors knew about the state convictions.

Pfaelzer had ruled the state convictions should not be disclosed to the jurors because it could prejudice their verdict. However, defence lawyers said at least six of the jurors knew about the state convictions.
Keating's hearing for a new trial on the federal case was scheduled for Nov. 25 in Los Angeles.
